title: Division of a scheme groupoid by a finite flat subrelation
statement: Let $S$ be a scheme and $(U,R,s,t,e,i,c)$ a groupoid scheme over $S$ [def-a1-groupoid-scheme], with $U$ affine. Let $P\to R$ be a monomorphism of schemes through which the unit factors, and on which inverse and composition restrict to a groupoid on $U$. Assume $s|_P,t|_P:P\to U$ are finite locally free [def-pc-finite-locally-free], $P\to U\times_SU$ is a monomorphism, and $j=(s,t):R\to U\times_SU$ is separated and locally quasi-finite. Here separated means its diagonal is a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion], locally quasi-finite means locally of finite type with discrete finite-type field fibres [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and monomorphism means injectivity on all test-scheme Hom sets. The fppf sheafification of $T\mapsto U(T)/P(T)$ is represented by an affine $S$-scheme $\bar U$. Its quotient map $q:U\to\bar U$ is finite locally free and surjective and identifies $P$ with $U\times_{\bar U}U$, preserving the source, target and composition. There is a groupoid scheme $(\bar U,\bar R,\bar s,\bar t,\bar e,\bar i,\bar c)$ over $S$ and a morphism of groupoid schemes whose object map is $q$, such that $R\cong(U\times_SU)\times_{\bar U\times_S\bar U}\bar R$ compatibly with all the groupoid operations. This is the meaning of restriction of the latter groupoid along $q$. The morphism $R\to\bar R$ sends $P$ into the unit: the square formed by the inclusion $P\to R$, the map $P\to\bar U$ equal to $q\circ s|_P=q\circ t|_P$, the map $R\to\bar R$ and $\bar e:\bar U\to\bar R$ commutes and is cartesian, so $P=R\times_{\bar R,\bar e}\bar U$ as subschemes of $R$, and under the restriction isomorphism this agrees with the identification of $P$ with $U\times_{\bar U}U$ above. Moreover two $T$-points $r,r'$ of $R$ have the same image in $\bar R(T)$ if and only if $r'=p\circ r\circ p'$ for some $p,p'\in P(T)$. Fibre products, affine schemes, fppf sheafification and surjectivity use [def-pc-fibre-product], [def-weil-affine-spectrum], [def-pc-fppf-site], [def-weil-pbc-sheafification], [def-weil-surjective-morphism].

proof.text: Since $s_P:P\to U$ is finite and $U$ is affine, $P$ is affine by finite-morphism permanence (b). The subgroupoid laws and monomorphism $P\to U\times_SU$ make $P(T)$ an equivalence relation on $U(T)$: identities give reflexivity, inverse gives symmetry, composition gives transitivity, and the monomorphism gives at most one arrow for each ordered pair. Apply the affine finite-flat-relation quotient theorem to $(U,P)$. It gives the affine $S$-scheme $\bar U$, the asserted sheafification, a finite locally free surjective $q$, and $P\simeq U\times_{\bar U}U$ with projections $s_P,t_P$. Composition on this kernel pair is forced to send $(z,y),(y,x)$ to $(z,x)$, since there is at most one $P$-arrow with specified endpoints.

The kernel-pair quotient-descent lemma applied to $(U,P,q)$ says that $\{q\}$ is an fppf covering. Every base change of $q$ is finite by finite-morphism permanence (a), and is an fppf covering by covering base change, hence flat and locally of finite presentation. Thus it is finite locally free by definition. Factoring $q^n:U^{\times_S n}\to\bar U^{\times_S n}$ into $n$ such base changes, finite-locally-free composition proves it finite locally free; it is surjective because each factor is a covering. Hence $q^n$ is an fppf covering. We use this for $n=2,3,4$ below. Base changes of these coverings are again fppf coverings, and are fpqc coverings by the fppf-to-fpqc lemma.

Use endpoint order $(t,s)$ in the construction; switching the factors identifies this with the order $(s,t)$ in the statement. Put $V=U\times_SU$ and $B=\bar U\times_S\bar U$. The kernel-pair identification gives $V\times_BV=P\times_SP$. For $a:x\to y$, $p:y'\to y$ and $p':x'\to x$ in $P(T)$, set $\varphi(a,(p,p'))=((p,p'),p^{-1}ap')$. This is a scheme morphism, being a composite of inverse, composition and fibre-product maps. Its inverse sends $((p,p'),a')$ to $(pa'(p')^{-1},(p,p'))$. On a triple overlap, successive transport by $(p_1,p'_1)$ and $(p_2,p'_2)$ gives $p_2^{-1}p_1^{-1}a p'_1p'_2=(p_1p_2)^{-1}a(p'_1p'_2)$, the direct transport. Thus this is a descent datum for $R\to V$ along $V\to B$. These formulas hold naturally for all test schemes, so also as scheme morphisms.

The singleton $\{V\to B\}$ is fppf by step 2. The structure map $R\to V$ is $j$, separated by hypothesis in the sense of [def-weil-proper-morphism], whose definition of separatedness is the one written in the statement. By hypothesis $j$ is locally of finite type and each fibre $R_v$, $v\in V$, is discrete. For $r\in R_v$ the point $\{r\}$ is then closed in $R_v$, and $r\in\overline{\{r'\}}$ forces $r'=r$ since $\{r'\}$ is closed too; the closed-fibre-point criterion [lem-sfb-closed-fibre-point-quasifinite-criterion] makes $j$ quasi-finite at $r$. Thus $j$ is locally quasi-finite in the sense of [pqf-def-quasifinite], as the descent theorem requires. Apply separated-locally-quasi-finite fppf effective descent to the datum of step 3. It gives a $B$-scheme $\bar R$ and an isomorphism $R\simeq V\times_B\bar R$ identifying $\varphi$ with canonical transport. Write $h:R\to\bar R$ for the projection. It is an fppf covering, since it is the base change of $V\to B$. In particular maps out of $\bar R$ can be descended, and their equality checked, along $h$ by representable fpqc descent and the fppf-to-fpqc lemma.

For $r,r'\in R(T)$ with $h(r)=h(r')$, their endpoint pairs give a $T$-point of $V\times_BV$. Thus there are unique $p:t(r')\to t(r)$ and $p':s(r')\to s(r)$ in $P(T)$. Canonical transport in the pullback $V\times_B\bar R$ keeps the $\bar R$ component fixed; the formula for $\varphi$ therefore gives $r'=p^{-1}rp'$. Conversely this formula is precisely a transport, so gives equal $h$-images. Replacing $p^{-1}$ by $p$ proves exactly the image characterization in the statement, with all compositions required to be defined. This argument uses actual $T$-points of the kernel pair, not a choice of local lifts of those points.

Define $\bar t,\bar s$ by the two structure projections $\bar R\to B$; then $\bar t h=qt$ and $\bar s h=qs$. To descend inverse, use $h i:R\to\bar R$. On the kernel pair of $h$, step 5 writes $r'=p^{-1}rp'$, and $(r')^{-1}=(p')^{-1}r^{-1}p$ has the same $h$-image as $r^{-1}$ by step 5. Representable fpqc descent along the fppf covering $h$ therefore gives a unique morphism $\bar i:\bar R\to\bar R$ satisfying $\bar i h=hi$. All maps are over $S$: their composites to $S$ agree after the same cover, where this follows from the original structure maps.

For $(y,x)\in U\times_{\bar U}U=P$, let $p:x\to y$ be its arrow. Then $e(y)=p e(x)p^{-1}$, so step 5 gives $he(y)=he(x)$. Representable fpqc descent along $q$ yields $\bar e:\bar U\to\bar R$ with $\bar e q=he$. Its source and target equal the identity, as can be checked after $q$. Moreover $p=p e(x)e(x)$ gives $h(p)=he(x)=\bar e(qx)$ by step 5. Thus the morphism on arrows already sends $P$ into the unit, as an equality of morphisms.

Put $D=\bar R\times_{\bar s,\bar U,\bar t}\bar R$, with arrows denoted $(A,B')$, and map it to $\bar U^{\times_S3}$ by $(\bar s(B'),\bar t(B')=\bar s(A),\bar t(A))$. Pull back $q^3$ to obtain the fppf cover $E\to D$. Its three object lifts $(x_0,x_1,x_2)$ and the pullback isomorphism of step 4 give unique arrows $b:x_0\to x_1$ and $a:x_1\to x_2$ lifting $(A,B')$. Hence $hc(a,b)$ is a morphism $E\to\bar R$. On $E\times_DE$, write $u_j:x_j\to x'_j$ for the unique $P$-arrows. Step 5 gives $a'=u_2au_1^{-1}$ and $b'=u_1bu_0^{-1}$, whence $a'b'=u_2ab u_0^{-1}$. Step 5 again gives $h(a'b')=h(ab)$. Representable fpqc descent yields a unique $\bar c:D\to\bar R$. Its source and target are the required ones by checking after $E\to D$.

The resulting operations satisfy the groupoid axioms. The unit laws and inverse laws can be checked on the covering $R\to\bar R$: choose the lifted endpoints, and they read $e(t(a))a=a$, $ae(s(a))=a$, $a^{-1}a=e(s(a))$ and $aa^{-1}=e(t(a))$ before applying $h$. For associativity, pull the two maps on composable triples back along the fppf covering obtained from $q^4$, lifting their four vertices. Their unique lifted arrows $a,b,c$ are composable and the two values are $h((ab)c)$ and $h(a(bc))$, equal by the original groupoid law. Equality descends by representable fpqc descent. The same formulas show preservation of every operation by $(q,h)$; the pullback isomorphism already identifies objects and arrows of the restriction, so it is an isomorphism of groupoid schemes.

Finally consider a $T$-point $(r,u)$ of $R\times_{\bar R,\bar e}\bar U$. Applying source and target gives $qs(r)=qt(r)=u$. The kernel-pair isomorphism of step 1 therefore gives a unique $p:s(r)\to t(r)$ in $P(T)$. Step 7 says $h(p)=\bar e(u)=h(r)$. In the pullback $R\simeq V\times_B\bar R$, the endpoints and $h$-image determine an arrow uniquely, so $r=p$. Conversely every $p\in P(T)$ defines such a pair, by step 7. These inverse correspondences use only fibre-product maps, naturally in $T$, and establish the claimed cartesian square as schemes. They also show that it agrees with $P\simeq U\times_{\bar U}U$.
